Site allocations under size and budget constraints

Source: R/design.R
balanced_allocation.Rd

Computes allocations under size and budget constraints. The continuous allocation maximizes the informativeness. With integer sizes and equal costs the allocation is optimal; with unequal costs the function uses a greedy rounding rule that need not find the integer optimum.

Usage

balanced_allocation(
  J,
  N = NULL,
  cost = NULL,
  budget = NULL,
  lower = NULL,
  upper = NULL,
  integer = TRUE
)

Arguments

J

Number of sites, a positive integer.

N

Total number of individuals, a positive number. Give N, for equal costs per individual, or cost and budget, not both. It must be an integer when integer = TRUE and is then allocated in full.

cost

Costs per individual in each site, positive numbers, one for all sites or one per site.

budget

Maximum budget, a positive number, in the units of cost.

lower, upper

Optional bounds on the site sizes, numbers, one for all sites or one per site.

integer

If TRUE (the default), the sizes are integers.

Value

A numeric vector of J site sizes, with the attributes total (the number of individuals) and, with costs, spent.

Details

The informativeness increases with the product of the site sizes when the constants \(\kappa_j\) are fixed, so the continuous allocation maximizes \(\sum_j \log n_j\) (Lee, 2026, Proposition 4 and Appendix E.3):

  • with equal costs and no bounds, every site gets \(N/J\).

  • with bounds \(L_j \le n_j \le U_j\), \(n_j = \min\{U_j, \max(L_j, t)\}\) with the level \(t\) that uses up \(N\).

  • with costs \(c_j\) and a budget \(B\), every site gets the same spending, \(n_j = B / (J c_j)\), clipped to the bounds in the same way.

With integer = TRUE, the continuous solution is rounded down and the remaining individuals (or budget) go one at a time to the sites where an individual adds most to \(\sum_j \log n_j\) per unit of cost. With equal costs the sizes then differ by at most 1 wherever the bounds allow; with unequal costs some of the budget can be left over. This greedy rule is optimal with equal costs, but is a heuristic with unequal costs. For example, with costs c(1, 3) and budget 10 it returns c(7, 1), whereas c(4, 2) has a larger product of site sizes at the same cost. Bounds are intersected with the positive integers before an integer allocation is computed; an infeasible request gives an error. A budget may also be left unused when every site has reached its upper bound.

References

Lee, J. (2026). The geometry of informativeness: A Bregman-centroid diagnostic for partial pooling in multisite trials. Unpublished manuscript.

See also

reliability_design() to compare a planned allocation with these, and vignette("planning").

Examples

balanced_allocation(J = 7, N = 100)
#> [1] 15 15 14 14 14 14 14
#> attr(,"total")
#> [1] 100
balanced_allocation(J = 5, N = 100, upper = c(10, 50, 50, 50, 50))
#> [1] 10 23 23 22 22
#> attr(,"total")
#> [1] 100
balanced_allocation(J = 4, cost = c(1, 1, 2, 4), budget = 400)
#> [1] 100 100  50  25
#> attr(,"total")
#> [1] 275
#> attr(,"spent")
#> [1] 400
